passage: The message reached Pallavi four times before lunch: a blurry photo of a white van and the words WARNING, CHILD-LIFTERS IN THE DISTRICT, SHARE WITH ALL MOTHERS. First from the college group, then from her aunt, then from two neighbours in Nandgaon. By the fourth time, Pallavi's stomach was tight. Four different people couldn't be wrong. She forwarded it to the family group and to the self-help group her mother ran. Uday, her cousin, replied within a minute: "Which district? Which date? This photo has been going round for years." Pallavi's cheeks went hot. "So you'd rather wait till something happens?" she typed. "Some people just don't care about children." She put the phone face down till evening. Then her mother read out the police station's notice: the photo was old, the child-lifter claim false. Pallavi deleted her forward and typed to both groups, "Please don't pass this on."

qa.q: How many times did the message reach Pallavi before lunch?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Uday questioned the message?
qa.a: Pallavi felt embarrassed and defensive; the hot cheeks and sharp reply show Uday's doubt felt like not caring about children.

qa.q: What could Pallavi have done just before forwarding, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi could have paused to ask Uday's kind of questions, which district and which date, since four forwards are not four separate sources.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after being told some people don't care about children?
qa.a: Uday may feel hurt and unfairly judged for asking simple questions, and might hesitate to question the next scary forward.

grounding: A young woman forwards a child-lifter warning because she has seen it many times, and treats her cousin's doubts as uncaring.

passage: In the student flat in Porto, Emil's phone buzzed again. Same message, fourth sender: URGENT! If a call comes from an unknown foreign number, DO NOT ANSWER. Just picking up empties your bank account!!! Tell everyone! His football coach had sent it. So had his aunt in Braga. Everyone was sending it, so it had to be real. Emil forwarded it to three groups and, for good measure, to Priscila across the table. She read it and snorted. "Picking up empties your account? How would that even work?" Emil felt a flash of irritation. "Fine, ignore it. Don't come to me when you're broke." "I'm just asking how—" "Everyone's warning each other, Priscila. You're the only one laughing." She stopped laughing. Later that night, Emil's bank sent every customer a notice: just answering a call cannot empty an account, and the forward was a hoax.

qa.q: Who had sent Emil the message besides the aunt in Braga?
qa.a: The football coach.

qa.q: What made Emil so sure the message was true?
qa.a: Emil kept getting it from different people, like the coach and the aunt, so the sheer number of forwards felt like proof.

qa.q: What question could Emil have asked before forwarding to three groups?
qa.a: Emil could have asked Priscila's question, how picking up could possibly empty an account, and looked for an official source before passing it on.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel after being called the only one laughing?
qa.a: Priscila may feel shut down and a little hurt, as if asking a sensible question made her seem careless.

grounding: A young man forwards a scare message because many people sent it, and treats Priscila's simple question as careless.

passage: Girls' hostel, Block C, 10 p.m. Rajni had heard the voice note five times: a man's worried voice saying bird flu had reached the city and anyone eating chicken this week would fall seriously ill. Her roommate had played it. Two floor groups had it. Her mother had sent it twice. Rajni forwarded it to the hostel group with STOP THE MESS CHICKEN in capitals. Vishal, the student mess secretary from the boys' block, replied: "Is there a notice from the health department? The mess buys from an inspected supplier." Rajni typed fast. "Sure, wait for a notice. Very caring, Vishal." Six people liked her reply. Only one liked Vishal's. Rajni felt certain, and a little proud, as she switched off the light. The next morning, the warden posted in the group: there was no health department alert about chicken in the city.

qa.q: Where was Rajni at 10 p.m.?
qa.a: In the girls' hostel, Block C.

qa.q: Why did Rajni feel certain and a little proud at the end?
qa.a: Rajni had heard the warning from many people and got more likes than Vishal, so the repetition and the approval felt like proof of being right and caring.

qa.q: At which point could Rajni have paused, and what would have helped?
qa.a: When Vishal asked about a health department notice, Rajni could have looked for one instead of treating the question as coldness.

qa.q: How might Vishal see getting only one like?
qa.a: Vishal may feel isolated and painted as uncaring for asking a reasonable question, and may be less willing to speak up next time.

grounding: A hostel student forwards a bird flu scare because it keeps reaching her, and treats a doubter as uncaring.

passage:
Dear Mahima,
I owe you an apology, and a letter feels better than a message for this.
On Sunday, when the forward said the dam upstream of Rampur had cracked and everyone should leave before dawn, I sent it to four groups within a minute. I had seen it nine times already. Nine people can't be wrong, I thought. When you replied, "Source? The district office hasn't said anything," I called you heartless in front of the whole family. I said, "If it's true and you did nothing, how will you feel?"
It wasn't true. The photo was of a different dam, from years ago. Nani packed a bag and sat up all night.
You were being careful, not cold. I'm sorry.
Deepak

qa.q: How many times had Deepak seen the dam message before forwarding it?
qa.a: Deepak had seen it nine times already.

qa.q: Why did Deepak call Mahima heartless for asking for a source?
qa.a: Seeing the message so often made it feel certain to Deepak, so doubting it seemed like not caring about people's safety.

qa.q: What could Deepak do the next time a scare message arrives again and again?
qa.a: Pause and check with an official source, like the district office Mahima mentioned, before forwarding it.

qa.q: What was the night like for Nani after the forward reached the family?
qa.a: Nani was frightened enough to pack a bag and sit up all night, a real cost of the false alarm.

grounding: A young adult forwards a scare message because it keeps arriving and treats the one doubter as cold.

passage: Nikita, you asked for a story about something dumb I did in first year. So this is Gautam's confession. During that heatwave, a message went round: "Phones are exploding in pockets above forty-five degrees! Share to save lives!" It came from my class group, my football group, my mother, my mother's friend. By evening I'd seen it about a dozen times, and each time it felt more obviously true. I forwarded it to everyone I knew. My flatmate Tsering just asked, "Is there any actual report?" And I got so annoyed. I told him, "People could get hurt and you want reports?" I made him feel like the villain. A week later, a lecturer showed us the photo was from a battery factory fire abroad. Tsering never said I told you so. I kind of wish he had.

qa.q: Who asked whether there was any actual report?
qa.a: Gautam's flatmate Tsering asked, "Is there any actual report?"

qa.q: What made the message feel more true to Gautam as the evening went on?
qa.a: Seeing it about a dozen times from different people made the repetition feel like proof.

qa.q: At which moment could Gautam have made a different choice?
qa.a: When Tsering asked for a report, Gautam could have paused and looked for one instead of snapping.

qa.q: How might Tsering have felt being treated like the villain for asking one question?
qa.a: Tsering might have felt hurt and unfairly judged, and perhaps less willing to question such messages again.

grounding: A young adult forwards a scare message seen many times and treats the doubting flatmate as careless.

passage:
Usha's phone buzzed for the twelfth time that morning. The same message, from different groups: "URGENT: Packet milk being sold in our city has plastic in it! Forward to save your family!!"
She'd seen it from her aunt, two college groups and the hostel group. So many people couldn't be wrong. She forwarded it to five more groups.
Her roommate Kavitha read it. "Where's this from? There's no name, no date, no news link."
"It doesn't matter. Everyone's sending it. You don't want to warn people?"
"I do. But I want it to be true first."
Usha felt a flash of irritation. How could Kavitha be so cold about something this serious? She didn't answer and sent it to her mother too.

qa.q: How many times had Usha's phone buzzed with the message that morning?
qa.a: It buzzed for the twelfth time that morning.

qa.q: Why did Usha feel irritated with Kavitha?
qa.a: Usha felt annoyed and anxious, because questioning the warning seemed cold and careless when so many people were sharing it.

qa.q: What could Usha do before forwarding a scare message?
qa.a: She could check for a name, date or official source, and look for news from a trusted health authority before sending it on.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel when Usha ignores her?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel frustrated and a little hurt, since caring about people is exactly why Kavitha wanted to check if the warning was true.

grounding: A young adult forwards an alarming food-safety message because many others have, and sees a doubting roommate as cold.

passage:
Last monsoon I forwarded a message I still think about. It said that sleeping near a phone charger could cause brain problems, and to "share with everyone you love."
I'd seen it from Mamma, from my college group, from a neighbour. Everywhere. By the fourth time, it just felt true. I forwarded it to thirty people.
My friend Uday replied, "Francis, is there a source?" I was annoyed. I actually thought, why does he always have to be so cold? Can't he just care?
Later he sent me a link from a health ministry page saying there was no such evidence. I felt my face go hot.
What I learned: seeing something ten times doesn't make it true. It just makes it familiar. And Uday wasn't cold. He was the only one checking.

qa.q: What did the message say could cause brain problems?
qa.a: It said that sleeping near a phone charger could cause brain problems.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when Uday asked for a source?
qa.a: Francis felt annoyed, even thinking Uday was cold, because the message felt true after seeing it so many times.

qa.q: What could Francis do the next time a scary message arrives?
qa.a: Francis could look for the original source or a health authority page before forwarding, as Uday did.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt sending the health ministry link?
qa.a: Uday may have felt a bit awkward but caring, wanting to stop a false fear without embarrassing Francis.

grounding: A young adult forwards a health scare because it appears everywhere, and sees a friend who questions it as cold.

passage:
Warden's note, boys' hostel. Tenzin, warden.
Last night Hrithik, second year, forwarded a message to the whole hostel group: "URGENT: men spraying perfume near colleges to kidnap students. Share with everyone!" By midnight it had been forwarded forty times, and several first-years were scared to walk to the library.
When I asked Hrithik about it this morning, he said, "It was in four groups already, sir. Everyone's sharing it, so it must be real." He added that when his roommate questioned it, others called the roommate careless.
I showed him the city police page, which lists the message as an old hoax. Hrithik looked embarrassed and posted a correction. I have asked the student council to run a short session on checking messages.

qa.q: How many times had the message been forwarded by midnight?
qa.a: Forty times.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel when he learned it was an old hoax?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, having trusted how often he saw the message rather than checking it.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do before forwarding the next alarming message?
qa.a: Check an official source like the city police page, since seeing a message often does not make it true.

qa.q: How was the roommate treated for doubting it?
qa.a: Others called the roommate careless, as if doubting meant not caring about safety.

grounding: A warden's note shows a student forwarding a scare message because it was everywhere, treating frequency as proof while a doubter was called careless.

Sunday.
Forwarded the message about "fruits injected with dye that damages kidneys" to the family group this morning. I'd seen it in five groups since Friday, so it didn't feel like a rumour any more; it felt like news. Masi thanked me with folded hands.
Kunal replied, "Source?" And honestly I felt annoyed. Why is he being so cold? People could get sick. Two aunties sent angry faces at him.
Tonight I finally searched it. The same photo had been going round for three years, with different fruits and different cities. The food safety department had called it false.
I haven't deleted the forward yet. I'm embarrassed. Tomorrow I'll post the correction.
Urmila

passage: By Thursday morning in Lagos, Emeka had seen the voice note eight times: a man, sounding very sure, saying phone chargers left plugged in overnight were exploding across the city, and three families had lost their homes that week. Emeka's mother had it. His football group had it. His cousin had sent it twice. So he forwarded it to his classmates with 'Please listen!!' His flatmate Ines, from Portugal, listened and frowned. 'Which families? Which area?' 'Everyone's sharing it.' 'That's not the same as it being true.' Emeka felt his face go hot. 'You'd rather wait for someone to burn?' She shrugged and went back to cooking. That evening Emeka searched the news for fires and found nothing matching. He looked at his forwarded message, now with eighty ticks, and didn't know what to do.

passage: The girls' hostel common room buzzed after dinner. A message was going round: 'Mess water contaminated, three students in hospital, DON'T drink it!' Dilnaz had it from four groups. Everyone at her table was talking about it. She forwarded it to her corridor group straight away. Then she typed it into the college-wide group too. Vishal, the student secretary, was at the warden's desk. He replied publicly: 'Checked with the warden and the infirmary. Nobody admitted. Water tested this morning. Please don't forward.' Dilnaz's cheeks burned. The table fell silent. 'He's just covering for the mess,' someone muttered. Dilnaz wanted to agree. But she also remembered she'd never asked where the message started. She stared at her own name above the forward, now shared a hundred times.

qa.q: Who did Vishal check with before replying?
qa.a: The warden and the infirmary.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz's cheeks burn?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt embarrassed and exposed, realising she had spread the message widely without checking where it started.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do next to limit the harm?
qa.a: She could post in the same groups that the claim was checked and was not true, and ask others to stop forwarding it.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel posting his reply?
qa.a: Vishal may feel responsible and a bit tense, knowing some students will see him as covering up rather than checking.

grounding: A young adult forwards an alarming health message because many others have, taking its frequency as proof.
